notes.b: Once a business has an idea, it still has to make sure the product or service fits what people actually want. Design thinking is a way of doing this. It starts from the end user, the person who will actually use the product (the customer may be someone else, such as a parent buying for a child).
points: The glossary definition is: "An innovative, non-linear approach to the development of products and services which focuses on solutions for the end user." Design thinking is a key term.
It is innovative because it treats problem solving as a creative process that generates new ideas, not only as analysis of existing data.
It is non-linear because teams move back and forth between phases. The phases are named in an order, but they are not completed once and then finished.
It is solution-centred because it aims to produce a practical answer to the user's problem.
It is person-centred because the user's needs, feelings and behaviour drive each decision.

It is iterative, which means the process repeats in cycles and each cycle refines the solution from the one before. Iterative (repeats, each cycle improving the last) is not the same as non-linear (steps can be revisited).
Design thinking supports idea development by reducing the risk of building something people do not want.
notes.tip: Define it with both halves of the glossary meaning: creative and non-linear, and focused on solutions for the end user. A common mistake is to say only 'creative'. Solution-centred and person-centred are different words, so do not treat them as one. If asked why it is iterative, give the cause and effect: each test or launch gives feedback that sends the team back, and the solution improves with each cycle.

notes.h: The four phases: clarify, ideate, develop, implement
notes.b: The specification names exactly four phases, in this order: clarify, ideate, develop and implement. Empathy research, problem statements, brainstorming, prototyping and testing are tools used inside these phases, not phases themselves.
points: 1. Clarify: understand the user and define the real problem before any solution is chosen.
2. Ideate: generate a wide range of possible solutions, then sort them and choose which to prototype.
3. Develop: turn the chosen idea into a prototype (a low-cost early version) and test it with real users.
4. Implement: launch the solution to customers, then monitor the results.
The order is only a guide. Results from testing or launch can send the team back to clarify, ideate or develop, so the phases form a loop and not a straight line of four steps.
notes.tip: Use the specification's phase names. Writing empathise, define, prototype and test as the four phases is a common mistake. Describing the process as a one-off sequence is another.

notes.b: Clarify means understanding the user and defining the real problem before any solution is chosen.
points: Empathy and user research means observing users, interviewing them and learning their needs, frustrations and habits. This is what makes the process person-centred.
A problem statement sums up what the user needs and why, and it guides every later phase.
Clarifying prevents a firm from solving the wrong problem, which is a common cause of product failure.
Ethical angle: user research must respect privacy and consent, because it collects personal information, which data protection law protects.
Ethical angle: designing for inclusion and accessibility from the start means the product works for all users, including those with disabilities.
Digital angle: online surveys let a firm reach many users quickly.
notes.tip: Expect the ethical, sustainability and digital themes to be assessed. User privacy and consent is a natural point to make for clarify.

notes.b: Ideate means generating a wide range of possible solutions before choosing one. Brainstorming here is a tool inside this phase.
points: Brainstorming produces many ideas quickly, with judgement held back until the list is complete, so that good ideas are not dismissed too early.
Ideas are then sorted against criteria such as user need and feasibility (whether the firm can actually make it), so the team chooses which ones to prototype.
Ideation works best when the group includes different perspectives, such as sales, design and users, because each sees different possibilities and problems.
Digital angle: collaboration software lets team members share and develop ideas even when they work in different places.
notes.tip: Do not confuse this with brainstorming as a source of business ideas. Here it is a phase tool for answering the problem stated in clarify.

notes.b: Develop turns the chosen idea into a prototype and tests it with real users. A prototype is a test version used to learn, not the launched product, and the test group is small.
points: Prototyping builds a simple, low-cost version of the product, such as a paper mock-up or clickable app screens, so mistakes are cheap to correct.
Testing shows how real users respond to the prototype and reveals problems the team did not expect.
Feedback from users is used to improve the design, and the cycle repeats until the design works well.
Developing is iterative because each test can send the team back to clarify the problem or to ideate again.
Sustainability angle: the team can design for durability, less packaging and less waste, and test the environmental cost of a design before it is made in large numbers.
Digital angle: clickable app prototypes let the team test a digital product without building it fully.

notes.b: Implement means launching the solution to customers and checking its results. Launch is not the end of the process.
points: Launch brings the product to customers through a planned marketing mix, including promotion, pricing and place (here they are only named).
After launch the firm monitors sales and customer feedback, which feeds into future improvements.
Implementation can reveal new problems, which send the team back to earlier phases.
Digital angle: user analytics show how customers use a digital product, and digital products can be updated continuously after implementation.
notes.tip: A common mistake is to treat the launch as the end. Include the monitoring of sales and feedback, and the loop back.

notes.h: Design thinking as a loop: a sample business
notes.b: The four phases form a loop, so each cycle improves the solution. A sample business shows how one product moves through all four phases and then back.
points: Sample business: a café chain notices long lunchtime queues. It clarifies the problem by observing customers, ideates ordering apps and counter layouts, develops a prototype app and tests it with regular customers.
If the app test shows that customers want to pay at a table, the team returns to ideate, and only then does it implement a rollout across the outlets.
After the rollout it monitors sales and customer feedback, and any new problem starts another cycle.

Second sample business for practice: a regional bakery launching a gluten-free range. It clarifies by interviewing customers about what they cannot buy, ideates recipes and packaging, tests samples with a small group of customers, then launches and monitors sales.
notes.tip: For a question on how a firm can use each phase to meet a client's expectations, name the four phases in order. For each, give what the firm does, the tool used and a link to the client's expectations, such as user needs, quality, cost and feedback. Use the firm's actual product from the question, not a copy of the phase list.

notes.b: Design thinking has clear advantages and some costs. Which matters more depends on the firm and the product.
points: Benefit: products that meet real user needs are more likely to succeed in the market.
Benefit: testing early reduces the cost of fixing faults after launch, because a fault in a prototype is cheaper to fix than one in a product already sold.
Drawback: the process takes time, and repeated testing can delay the launch.
Drawback: research with a small group of users may not represent the whole market.
Drawback: the firm needs staff with the right skills, and running the process may require training.
Evaluation: a small firm facing a fast-moving competitor may find the delay costly, while a firm with a complex product gains most from early testing.
notes.tip: For a discuss question, give three or four developed points with their effect on a small firm (cost of fixing faults, time to launch, how representative the research is, skills needed) and finish with a judgement.

keyTerms.definition: An innovative, non-linear approach to solving problems that focuses on solutions for the end user through four phases.
Repeating a process in cycles, with each cycle refining the result of the one before.
An approach in which the needs, feelings and behaviour of the user guide each decision.
An approach that aims to deliver a practical answer to the user's problem, rather than an abstract analysis.
The ability to understand another person's needs, feelings and experiences, built in design thinking through observation and interviews.
A short, clear description of the user's need and the problem to be solved, which guides the rest of the process.
A simple, low-cost early version of a product used to test ideas before full production.
A process in which the steps can be revisited in any order, rather than completed once in sequence.

First phase: aim and main tools

factCards.term: Second phase: aim and main tool
factCards.definition: Ideate, which aims to generate many possible solutions, mainly through brainstorming.

Products that meet real needs, and early testing that reduces the cost of later fixes.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery wants to launch a gluten-free range. Using the four design thinking phases in order, describe what the firm would do in each phase.
questions.model: In the clarify phase the bakery would observe and interview people who avoid gluten, to learn what they need from bread and cakes, such as taste, texture and labelling they trust, and it would write a problem statement, for example that coeliac customers lack tasty gluten-free bakery products they can buy locally. In the ideate phase the team would brainstorm recipes, flours and product formats, such as loaves, scones and sponge cakes, and would screen them against cost, shelf life and the bakery's skills. In the develop phase the bakery would make prototype recipes in small batches and test them with a panel of customers, collecting feedback on taste, price and texture, then adjust the recipes. In the implement phase it would launch the range in its shops, promote it through its social media and local customers, and track sales and reviews. The process is iterative, so if reviews show that customers want a larger loaf, the firm would return to develop or ideate rather than treating the launch as final.

questions.prompt: Explain why design thinking is described as iterative.
questions.model: Design thinking is iterative because the process repeats in cycles rather than running once in a straight line. Each test or launch produces feedback that sends the team back to an earlier phase, so the solution improves with each cycle.

questions.prompt: Discuss two benefits and one drawback of design thinking for a small Irish firm.
questions.model: The first benefit is that the firm builds products that meet real customer needs, which improves the chance of success in a competitive market and reduces wasted spending on products nobody buys. The second benefit is that early prototype testing finds faults while they are cheap to fix, rather than after an expensive launch. The drawback is time: a small firm with limited staff may find that repeated testing delays its launch, which can matter if a competitor reaches the market first.
